title: Sowing radish
subtitle: A three-week-turnover crop sown in short rows through spring and summer
excerpt: Radish is the fastest-maturing vegetable in the UK kitchen garden, going from seed to edible root in three to four weeks in summer. It is useful as a catch crop between slower plants and as a row marker for slower-germinating seeds.
sourceNotes: Mrs Beeton, Book of Household Management (1861), salads section. RHS radish growing guide (rhs.org.uk). USDA agricultural extension service notes on radish production, public domain.

glossaryTerms.definition: A fast-maturing crop grown in a bed between the clearing of one main crop and the planting of the next. Radish, lettuce, and spring onions are common catch crops. They make use of ground that would otherwise sit empty and weed-prone.

content.text: Radish grows from seed to edible root in three to four weeks in summer. It is the standard

for beds between larger plantings and a useful marker for slow-germinating seeds like parsnip and carrot. Sow a short row every two weeks from March to September and you always have something to pull.

March through September, with a short row every two weeks. Spring and autumn sowings take three to five weeks to mature; midsummer sowings take three weeks or less. Avoid large sowings that mature all at once: twenty radishes eaten the same week is a waste. A row of 15 to 20 seeds every fortnight is more useful.

Full sun for the fastest growth; partial shade is acceptable and slows the crop slightly in summer, giving a longer harvest window before bolting. Light, moist soil gives the smoothest, roundest roots. Heavy clay produces irregular shapes but still edible roots. Grow radish between rows of slower crops: between parsnips, between leeks, under sweet corn.

Sow 1 to 1.5 cm deep, one seed every 2.5 cm, in rows 15 cm apart. No thinning needed if sown thinly. Pull as soon as the roots reach eating size (1.5 to 2.5 cm diameter for salad radishes). Leave them too long and they go pithy and hollow in the centre.

Germination is fast: three to five days in a warm seedbed, seven to ten days in cold spring soil. The seedlings emerge as two oval seed leaves on a short stem. Germination failure is rare; if nothing shows after two weeks the seed has rotted, usually from cold wet soil.

Water in dry weather; drought makes the roots pithy and hot-tasting. Keep the bed weed-free. Harvest promptly when roots reach size: they deteriorate quickly if left in the ground. In summer, check every two or three days.

attrs.heading: Common problems
attrs.intro: A quick crop has short problems, but these are the main ones.

items.symptom: Plants run to seed without forming roots
items.cause: Too warm, too dry, sown too thickly, or left too long after maturity.
items.fix: Sow thinly. Water consistently. Pull roots promptly at eating size. For summer crops, choose slower-bolting varieties.
Cover with fine insect-proof mesh. Light infestations don't affect root development on a fast crop.

items.symptom: Roots pithy or hollow in the centre
items.cause: Left too long after reaching maturity, or drought stress.
items.fix: Harvest promptly. Water consistently in dry weather.
